ELECTRIC RELIABILITY COUNCIL OF TEXAS, INC.’S 
COMMENTS REGARDING PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) respectfully submits these comments regarding the Public Utility Commission of Texas’s (Commission) proposal for publication (PFP) of amendments to 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §§ 25.192 and § 25.193, and new 16 TAC § 25.252.  ERCOT generally defers to the Commission’s judgment as to the appropriate allocation of transmission costs and provides these comments only to identify several provisions relating to ERCOT’s calculation of coincident peak load values that may benefit from further clarification.  ERCOT also provides a response to Commission Staff’s question regarding the impact of transmission capacity reservations on resource adequacy reports and transmission planning studies.  
RESPONSE TO STAFF’S QUESTIONS
ERCOT provides the following response to Staff’s Question 6:  
If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and transmission planning studies?  

ERCOT Response: 

ERCOT’s resource adequacy reports should accurately reflect projected load and generation to the greatest extent possible.  Accordingly, if a large load customer’s development timeline changes, the resource adequacy reports should generally reflect that change irrespective of whether that load may have been allocated transmission capacity for an earlier period under an interconnection study process.  If a load will not materialize on its original timeline, it should not be reflected in resource adequacy assessments for any period before it energizes or increases its demand.
For transmission planning, a different approach is necessary if reservations or allocations of capacity are allowed.  A reservation of transmission capacity would require that the large load customer’s demand be factored into planning studies for the year of the reservation even if the customer later delays its desired energization schedule beyond that reservation year.  This is so that the transmission needs associated with any other new load seeking interconnection could be properly evaluated without affecting the reserved or assigned capacity. For clarity, ERCOT underscores that any reservation of transmission capacity would apply only for transmission planning purposes and would not amount to a right to firm transmission service for operational purposes.  ERCOT’s protocols do not currently recognize firm transmission service rights.  
COMMENTS ON PROPOSED RULE
16 TAC § 25.192(f)(1)(B): Calculation of DSP 12CP Load Adjustment
Subsection (f)(1)(B) describes the adjustment to the DSP 12CP Load values ERCOT would be required to calculate using the proposed large load minimum billing demand value.  As proposed, ERCOT would calculate the adjustment 
by adding to each measured DSP 12CP load, for each large load customer of that DSP, the difference between that customer’s large load minimum billing demand, as described in §25.193 of this title . . . and that customer’s measured 12CP load, adjusted for line losses as appropriate and annualized across the annual period for large load customers initiating their connection within the period or for large load customers which have increased their contracted peak demand or NCP demand within the period.
ERCOT requests additional clarification to ensure its calculation aligns with the Commission’s policy objectives.  ERCOT reads this provision to require the adjustment for line losses to be applied to both the large load billing demand value and the customer’s 12CP load value.  If that is accurate, ERCOT notes that it is not aware of any means to apply line losses to a large load minimum billing demand value that is based on contracted peak demand.  ERCOT’s existing processes assign losses to retail electronic service identifiers (ESI IDs).  However, if the large load customer does not yet have an assigned ESI ID (which is plausible in a case where ERCOT is using a large load’s contracted peak demand as its large load minimum billing demand value because the customer has not yet energized its facility), then ERCOT does not have any means of calculating or assigning line losses to that customer.  ERCOT therefore recommends that it be required to apply losses to a large load minimum billing demand value only when that value is determined using the load’s non-coincident peak demand or 12CP demand.  
ERCOT is also uncertain how to interpret the language in (f)(1)(B) requiring the difference between a customer’s large load minimum billing demand and 12CP load values to be “annualized across the annual period for large load customers initiating their connection within the period or for large load customers which have increased their contracted peak demand or NCP demand within the period.”  If this language is intended to require application of the highest large load minimum billing demand value across all months of the 12-month period used for calculating the 12CP load, ERCOT would recommend that this provision be rephrased to state that more explicitly.  For example, the rule might require that, “For each large load customer, ERCOT must use the highest large load minimum billing demand value identified during the 12-month period used to determine 12CP load under this subsection in calculating the adjustment for each month in that period.”  If that is not the intention, ERCOT would request further clarification of the intended purpose.
The Commission may wish to consider another potential clarification relating to the scenario where a large load customer’s contracted peak demand is used to determine the large load minimum billing demand under 16 TAC § 25.193(d).  If a large load customer delayed its energization date beyond the 12-month period used to calculate the 12CP load, resulting in a contracted peak demand that exceeds the non-coincident and 12CP load values, but the customer’s contracted peak demand value did not change during that 12-month period, the customer would presumably neither be “initiating [its] connection” nor “increasing [its] contracted peak demand or NCP demand” within the 12-month period.  In that situation, ERCOT would not read the proposed rule to require the large load minimum billing demand to be “annualized across the annual period.” If that is not what is contemplated, the Commission may wish to broaden the language to ensure the application of the minimum billing demand value occurs even when the contracted peak demand value does not change during the 12-month period.  
		ERCOT further notes that subsection (f)(1)(B) appears to require ERCOT to calculate the large load minimum billing demand for each large load customer indefinitely while proposed 16 TAC § 25.193(d)(3) and 16 TAC § 25.252(e)(2)(ii) would excuse that customer (and its REP) from paying the demand charge after a period of 20 years from the date the facilities are made available to the customer.  If ERCOT’s duty to include the large load minimum billing demand in the 12CP load calculation does not terminate, a large load customer’s DSP would continue to be allocated costs based on that customer’s large load minimum billing demand even when the DSP has no means of recovering the cost from its customer under the proposed rule.  If that is not the Commission’s intent, the Commission may wish to clarify the rule to impose a similar expiration on ERCOT’s duty to adjust 12CP load in the manner described in (f)(1)(B).  
		Additionally, the potential for using contracted peak demand as a customer’s large load minimum billing demand in subsection (f)(1)(B) introduces a risk that the contracted peak demand value could decrease due to an amendment to the customer’s interconnection agreement after the transmission facilities needed to serve the customer have been constructed.  In that scenario, using a lower contracted peak demand value would reduce the adjustment to the DSP’s 12CP demand for that large load customer relative to the contracted demand levels that may have contributed to the need for transmission investment.  The Commission may wish to consider whether subsection (f)(1)(B) should be revised to ensure that the contracted peak demand values that drove the transmission investment are used in calculating the large load minimum billing demand value.
		Finally, ERCOT notes that, for some existing large load customers, ERCOT does not have contracted peak demand values as described in proposed 16 TAC § 25.194.  Moreover, the interconnection agreements from which these values are proposed to be derived do not all identify contracted MW values in the same manner.  Commission rules or ERCOT protocols will need to be revised to ensure that ERCOT obtains this information from all large load customers and that the information is provided in a standardized fashion.  If the Commission would prefer that ERCOT address this in its protocols, it would be helpful for the rule to reflect this, just as 16 TAC § 25.192(f) already recognizes that protocol revisions will be necessary to implement the 12CP load calculation.
	16 TAC § 25.192(f)(1)(A): Non-IOU DSP Data Provision Obligations
	As proposed, subsection (f)(1)(A) would require each non-IOU DSP to provide settlement quality meter data to ERCOT for each large load customer in the DSP’s service territory.  ERCOT agrees with this provision but recommends revisions to require non-IOU DSPs to provide ERCOT other information it needs to calculate the large load minimum billing demand value for each large load customer.  Specifically, non-IOU DSPs should be required to provide ERCOT the non-coincident peak load and 12CP load values for each large load customer in its service territory, consistent with the requirements of subsection (f)(1)(B).  This revision is needed because ERCOT does not meter individual customers in non-IOU DSP areas and therefore does not have the ability to independently determine these values for those customers.  The rule should also require non-IOU DSPs to adjust those load values to reflect the impact of line losses and the annualized adjustment, as contemplated in (f)(1)(B).
16 TAC § 25.193(d)(2): Use of Same 12-month Lookback Period for All Three Parameters in Large Load Minimum Billing Demand Calculation 
		Subsection (d)(2) of proposed 16 TAC § 25.193 provides that the large load minimum billing demand is calculated as the greater of 
the large load customer’s contracted peak demand, as defined in §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards); 
the highest non-coincident peak demand placed by the large load customer on the system in the past year; or
the large load customer’s 12CP demand consistent with the most recent ERCOT 12CP intervals, as defined in §25.192 of this title (relating to Transmission Service Rates).  
		Proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(f)(1)(B) would require ERCOT to use the large load minimum billing demand to adjust a large load customer’s demand in calculating each DSP’s share of the ERCOT 12CP load.  While proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(f)(1) proposes a 12-month period ending September 30 as the annual period of review for 12CP demand under paragraph (C) above, it is not clear that a similar lookback period applies to ERCOT’s review of the large load customer’s contracted peak demand or non-coincident peak demand.  In fact, 16 TAC § 25.193(d)(2)(B) proposes that ERCOT will consider non-coincident peak demand over “the past year,” which may or may not align with the 12-month lookback required by proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(f)(1).  And 16 TAC § 25.193(d)(2)(A) does not specify a period over which the large load customer’s contracted peak demand must be evaluated.
		ERCOT strongly recommends that its calculation of large load minimum billing demand should use the same lookback period for the contracted peak demand and non-coincident peak demand calculations that it uses for the 12CP load calculation.  More specifically, ERCOT suggests that the Commission require ERCOT to use the 12-month period ending on September 30 of the year of ERCOT’s analysis for all three parameters in 16 TAC § 25.193(d)(1), consistent with the period specified in 16 TAC § 25.192(b)(4).  This will ensure consistency in comparing the different parameters.  
16 TAC § 25.192(b)(4): Determination of 30-Minute Intervals Used in ERCOT 12CP Load Calculation
		Subsection (b)(4) of proposed 16 TAC 25.192 would require ERCOT to identify the 30-minute interval with the highest system demand in each month.  This could be interpreted to require calculation of total demand over a rolling 30-minute period that begins at any moment in time, which would exceed ERCOT’s current capabilities based on the load data it receives from TDSPs.  For its settlement and data aggregation purposes, ERCOT currently collects load information from individual TDSPs for each clock settlement interval—i.e., a 15-minute period that corresponds to the beginning of each hour or 15, 30, or 45 minutes afterward.  ERCOT’s systems are not equipped to evaluate individual DSP loads over a rolling 30-minute period that does not align with these 15-minute clock intervals—e.g., a period beginning at 5:07 p.m. and ending at 5:37 p.m.  
		To avoid ambiguity about which period of time is intended, and to align the rule with ERCOT’s existing systems, ERCOT recommends that the Commission clarify this provision to require that the beginning of the 30-minute interval align with either a 15-minute clock interval or or a 30-minute clock interval.   Under a 30-minute clock interval, ERCOT would evaluate the total MWh load for each half-hour period in the month, beginning at the top of each hour or the middle of each hour.  For example, for the hour between 5:00 and 6:00 p.m., ERCOT would evaluate the periods from 5:00 to 5:30 and from 5:30 to 6:00 (ERCOT would not evaluate the period from 5:15 to 5:45).  Whether the 30-minute interval begins with a 15-minute clock interval or a 30-minute clock interval, ERCOT would interpret the proposed rule to require it to determine the average peak MW load value during the one 30-minute period with the greatest MWh consumption during that month and would use that MW value for the month in its ERCOT 12CP load calculation.  
16 TAC § 25.192(f): Protocol Adoption and Implementation
		Subsection (f)(1) of proposed 16 TAC § 25.192 provides that “[t]he measurement of the ERCOT system monthly peak demand for purposes of determining the ERCOT 12CP intervals and the determination of the DSP demand values that coincide with the ERCOT 12CP intervals must be in accordance with ERCOT protocols.”  Because ERCOT’s protocols do not currently reflect a 12CP allocation methodology, ERCOT reads this provision to provide that revisions to ERCOT protocols must be adopted and implemented before ERCOT can apply a 12CP allocator.  ERCOT further assumes that the time needed for the stakeholder consideration and ERCOT implementation of the required protocol revisions would effectively require a delay to the implementation of the entirety of Rule 25.192, if not all three rules.  If the Commission agrees, it may be helpful to provide greater clarity and transparency in the final rule or preamble as to the anticipated scope of the rule provisions that are subject to delay due to the need for protocol revisions. 


16 TAC § 25.192(f)(1): Clarifying Revisions
		ERCOT proposes the following revisions to 16 TAC § 25.192(f)(1) to further clarify the period of time required for ERCOT’s 12CP Load calculation:  
No later than December 1 of each year, ERCOT must determine and file with the commission the current year’s DSP 12CP load for each DSP, based on the ERCOT 12CP intervals during the 12-month period ending on the last day of the immediately preceding September.  ERCOT must also include in this filing the ERCOT 12CP load for the current year same 12-month period.
ERCOT also proposes clarifying revisions to 16 TAC § 25.192(f)(1)(B), as follows:
For each large load customer, the adjustment under this subparagraph must commence for each MW at the level of available service at the time it that level of service is made available to the customer, irrespective of whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity.
If the Commission concurs with these revisions to subsection (f)(1)(B), it may wish to consider similar revisions to 16 TAC § 25.193(d)(3), which uses similar phrasing. 
 II. CONCLUSION
ERCOT appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments on the Commission’s proposed rule.  ERCOT would be pleased to provide any information the Commission may find helpful to its consideration and adoption of a final rule in this proceeding.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF ERCOT’S COMMENTS

ERCOT’s Response to Staff’s Questions: 
Question 6: ERCOT’s resource adequacy reports should reflect actual expected load, not transmission reservations. If a large load delays or changes its development timeline, the load should not appear in resource adequacy assessments until it is expected to materialize.
However, transmission planning must continue to include the load in the year for which transmission capacity was reserved so ERCOT can ensure sufficient infrastructure for all loads in the area.
Comments on Proposed Rule:
ERCOT cannot calculate losses for contracted load that has not energized; the rule should apply losses only when the billing demand is based on actual NCP or 12CP demand.
The Commission should clarify what it means to “annualize” the difference between minimum billing demand and 12CP load.
The Commission should consider whether the 20-year limit on demand charges should also apply to ERCOT’s calculation of the large load minimum billing demand value. Reductions in contracted peak demand could lower DSP allocations below levels used to justify transmission investment.
Non-IOU DSPs should be required to provide ERCOT NCP and 12CP load values for large load customers in their service territories.
ERCOT recommends using the same 12-month period ending September 30 for contracted peak demand, NCP demand, and 12CP demand to ensure consistent calculation of the minimum billing demand.
The Commission should clarify that ERCOT will use either 15-minute clock intervals or 30-minute clock intervals for the ERCOT 12CP calculation, aligning with ERCOT’s current capabilities.
ERCOT interprets the proposed rule to require Protocol revisions before implementing the 12CP allocator and suggests greater clarity on what revisions must be adopted before the rule can take effect.

clock interval, ERCOT would interpret the proposed rule to require it to determine the average

peak MW load value during the one 30-minute period with the greatest MWh consumption during

that month and would use that MW value for the month in its ERCOT 12CP load calculation.

        E. 16 TAC § 25.192(f): Protocol Adoption and Implementation
        Subsection (f)(1) of proposed 16 TAC § 25.192 provides that "[tlhe measurement of the

ERCOT system monthly peak demand for purposes of determining the ERCOT 12CP intervals

and the determination of the DSP demand values that coincide with the ERCOT 12CP intervals

must be in accordance with ERCOT protocols." Because ERCOT's protocols do not currently

reflect a 12CP allocation methodology, ERCOT reads this provision to provide that revisions to

ERCOT protocols must be adopted and implemented before ERCOT can apply a 12CP allocator.

ERCOT further assumes that the time needed for the stakeholder consideration and ERCOT

implementation of the required protocol revisions would effectively require a delay to the

implementation of the entirety of Rule 25.192, if not all three rules. If the Commission agrees, it

may be helpful to provide greater clarity and transparency in the final rule or preamble as to the

anticipated scope of the rule provisions that are subject to delay due to the need for protocol

revisions.

                    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF ERCOT'S COMMENTS

ERCOT's Response to Staff's Questions:

Question 6: ERCOT's resource adequacy reports should reflect actual expected load, not
transmission reservations. If a large load delays or changes its development timeline, the load
should not appear in resource adequacy assessments until it is expected to materialize.
However, transmission planning must continue to include the load in the year for which
transmission capacity was reserved so ERCOT can ensure sufficient infrastructure for all loads in
the area.
Comments on Proposed Rule:

    •   ERCOT cannot calculate losses for contracted load that has not energized; the rule should
        apply losses only when the billing demand is based on actual NCP or 12CP demand.

    •   The Commission should clarify what it means to "annualize" the difference between
        minimum billing demand and 12CP load.

    •   The Commission should consider whether the 20-year limit on demand charges should also
        apply to ERCOT's calculation ofthe large load minimum billing demand value. Reductions
        in contracted peak demand could lower DSP allocations below levels used to justify
        transmission investment.

    •   Non-IOU DSPs should be required to provide ERCOT NCP and 12CP load values for large
        load customers in their service territories.

    •   ERCOT recommends using the same 12-month period ending September 30 for contracted
        peak demand, NCP demand, and 12CP demand to ensure consistent calculation of the
        minimum billing demand.

    •   The Commission should clarify that ERCOT will use either 15-minute clock intervals or
        30-minute clock intervals for the ERCOT 12CP calculation, aligning with ERCOT's
        current capabilities.

    •   ERCOT interprets the proposed rule to require Protocol revisions before implementing the
        12CP allocator and suggests greater clarity on what revisions must be adopted before the
        rule can take effect.
